item.title: A bookmarklet highlighting roles that must never have author-provided names
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: This bookmarklet highlights elements with name-prohibited roles.
item.content:encoded: A bookmarklet that highlights ARIA roles where author-provided accessible names are forbidden. A practical way to find naming errors and better understand ARIA naming rules.

item.title: Using the browser console for accessibility testing - Part 2
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: Learn how to use browser console scripts to test aria-invalid, aria-hidden, aria-expanded, tabindex, accessible names, required fields and name-prohibited roles.
item.content:encoded: Build on browser-based accessibility testing techniques using the console. This article explores additional JavaScript snippets that help inspect accessible names, descriptions, roles, states and properties directly in the browser.

item.title: Where can aria-label and aria-labelledby be used for naming elements?
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: A simple explanation of how and where to use aria-label and aria-labelledby correctly.
item.content:encoded:
A simple explanation of how aria-label and aria-labelledby work, where they can be used, and why some elements and roles do not support accessible naming.

item.title: Three accessibility assumptions
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: Three accessibility assumptions about the DOM, accessibility trees, and screen reader output that shape how we test, debug, and interpret results.
item.content:encoded:
Accessibility tooling encourages us to build simplified mental models of how browsers and assistive technologies work. This article unpacks three common accessibility assumptions about the DOM, accessibility trees, and screen reader speech output, and explains why real-world testing often feels unpredictable despite best practices.

Read the full article

item.title: What is the minimum markup needed to create a modal?
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: A practical look at the minimum HTML needed to create a modal dialog, with an optional enhancement based on real user testing.
item.content:encoded:
Is it possible to build a modal dialog without any JavaScript at all? In this article, we’ll look at two small experiments that explore what the platform can already do, and what small enhancements can improve the experience for real users.

Option 1: what is the minimum needed for a modal to work?

Option 2: what is the minimum we can do to make this modal easier to understand for real users?

Read the full article

item.title: Do screen readers announce “bullet” when a list uses list-style: none?
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: An explanation of why list-style: none removes bullet announcements in screen readers by tracing browser, accessibility tree, and screen reader behaviour.
item.content:encoded:
If you remove bullets from an unordered list using list-style: none, do screen readers still announce “bullet” before each list item?

At first glance, this feels like a screen reader question. But the answer actually lives deeper in the browser pipeline:

To explore this, we’ll start with a simple unordered list, then follow what happens as it moves through the browser, into the accessibility tree, and finally into screen reader output.

Read the full article

item.title: Is aria-label allowed on static elements?
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: An examination of how aria-label behaves on static elements across browsers, and why real-world support differs from common assumptions.
item.content:encoded:
In this article, we examine how aria-label behaves on static elements in practice, across browsers and platforms, and why real-world behaviour is often more nuanced than common assumptions suggest.

The examples include clearly flagged bad-practice patterns alongside legitimate use cases, to show what is exposed at the accessibility API level — and why exposure alone does not imply recommendation.

Read the full article

item.title: How can you tell what's allowed inside each HTML element?
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: A practical guide to reading the HTML Living Standard to check where elements can be used and what they are allowed to contain.
item.content:encoded:
The HTML Living Standard documents every element. This includes: where elements can appear, what they are allowed to contain, which attributes they support and how they behave in the DOM.

Read the full article

item.title: HTML content categories
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: HTML content categories define where elements can appear and what they’re allowed to contain with a clear, rules-based approach that improves validity, accessibility, and maintainability.
item.content:encoded:
Modern HTML, defined in the HTML Living Standard, groups elements into content categories.

These categories do not control how elements look. They describe how elements fit into the document structure and how they relate to the elements around them.

Read the full article

item.title: People with reduced vision: technology settings and possible impacts
item.dc:creator: Russ Weakley
item.description: How people with low vision adjust system settings, browsers, and apps. Six key categories designers and developers should understand.
item.content:encoded:
Many people experience reduced vision at some point in their lives. This might be temporary, gradual, or permanent. It can affect how clearly someone sees text, images, and user interface elements on screens.

Understanding these options is essential for anyone building digital products.
